items.source_name: FEMA — National Incident Management System / Incident Command System
items.locator: ICS overview: a standardized, on-scene, all-hazards approach to command, control and coordination that integrates facilities, equipment, personnel, procedures and communications within a common organizational structure.
items.version: Current FEMA NIMS/ICS training content live-rechecked 2026-08-15; NCSBN 2026 Management of Care emergency-response relevance checked.
items.stem: What is the primary purpose of the Incident Command System during a hospital response to a large emergency?

options.A: Use a permanent command structure that replaces normal hospital leadership after the incident.
options.B: Allow departments to manage the incident independently without shared objectives or resource coordination.
options.C: Limit command and coordination to external police, fire, and emergency medical agencies.
options.D: Use a standardized scalable structure for command, coordination, resources, and communication during the incident.

items.rationale: FEMA describes ICS as a standardized, scalable system for command, control, coordination, resources, personnel, facilities, and communication. Option D is correct. It is temporary and incident-focused, promotes coordination rather than independent silos, and is used across sectors including healthcare.
items.finding: Round-2 review replaced the short distractors with parallel incident-management structures so the correct definition is not signaled by length.

items.locator: Management of Care activity statements: establish priorities for care, facilitate referrals and follow-up, collaborate with the interprofessional team, use resources, and provide care within legal scope; clinical judgment is integrated throughout the plan.
items.version: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A telephone-triage nurse receives a caller reporting new chest pressure and shortness of breath. Which action best reflects the RN's role?

options.A: Diagnose acute coronary syndrome from the telephone history and provide a definitive diagnosis to the caller.
options.B: Perform a focused assessment, recognize a possible emergency, and direct urgent evaluation according to protocol and scope.
options.C: Complete a detailed lifetime history before deciding whether emergency evaluation is needed.
options.D: Recommend a prescription drug for chest pain without an authorized order, protocol, or prescriber involvement.

items.rationale: Telephone triage requires nursing assessment and clinical judgment within scope, not remote definitive diagnosis or unauthorized prescribing. New chest pressure with dyspnea can represent an emergency, so Option B appropriately prioritizes urgent evaluation. A exceeds the information available, C delays care, and D exceeds scope absent an authorized mechanism.
items.finding: Round-2 review rebuilt all four telephone-triage actions at comparable clinical granularity while preserving mandatory NCSBN scope and prioritization principles.

items.locator: Management of Care — Advocacy/Client Rights activity statements: advocate for client rights and preferences, provide information needed for informed decisions, facilitate referrals/continuity, and collaborate with the care team.
items.version: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A client wants a second opinion before a major elective operation. Which nursing response is most appropriate?

options.A: Discourage another opinion because it may damage the therapeutic relationship.
options.B: Tell the client that only the surgeon can decide whether a second opinion is allowed.
options.C: Support the client's choice and help identify how records or referrals can be obtained.
options.D: Advise the client to have the operation first and seek another opinion afterward.

items.rationale: Supporting an informed client choice and helping coordinate information or referral is consistent with nursing advocacy and client rights. Option C is correct. A and B undermine autonomy, and D defeats the purpose of seeking another opinion before an elective decision.
items.finding: Fresh audit used the mandatory NCSBN Management of Care source because the tested nursing competency is advocacy/client rights, not physician ethics.

items.source_name: National Institute on Aging — Advance Care Planning: Advance Directives for Health Care
items.locator: Durable power of attorney for health care section: names a health care proxy/agent to make health care decisions if the person cannot communicate or make decisions; state rules and document scope apply.
items.version: Current NIH/NIA advance-care-planning guidance live-rechecked 2026-08-15; NCSBN 2026 Management of Care advance-directive relevance checked.
items.stem: Which statement best describes a durable power of attorney for health care?

options.A: Use the document only to authorize financial decisions and not health care choices.
options.B: Use the designated agent to make health care decisions if the person cannot decide or communicate, within the document and law.
options.C: Treat the document as equivalent to a DNR order that applies only during cardiopulmonary arrest.
options.D: Transfer all decision-making authority to the agent immediately after signing, even while the person remains capable.

items.rationale: A durable power of attorney for health care designates a proxy or agent to make health care decisions if the person becomes unable to decide or communicate, subject to the document and applicable state law. Option B is correct. It is distinct from financial authority and DNR orders, and it does not automatically displace a capable person's decisions.
items.finding: Round-2 review made the four advance-directive interpretations parallel and comparable while preserving the document-scope and applicable-law qualification.

items.locator: DNR scope: directs providers not to perform CPR if breathing or heartbeat stops; it is specific to CPR and does not itself stop other treatments such as pain medicine or nutrition.
items.version: Current MedlinePlus/NLM patient-instruction content live-rechecked 2026-08-15; NCSBN 2026 advance-directive/client-rights relevance checked.
items.stem: A client has a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order. Which statement correctly explains its scope?

options.A: All routine medications and nursing care must stop.
options.B: Only comfort care may be provided.
options.C: CPR is withheld if breathing or heartbeat stops, but other indicated treatments may still be provided.
options.D: Chest compressions are withheld, but defibrillation and resuscitation drugs must still be used.

items.rationale: A DNR order applies to cardiopulmonary resuscitation when breathing or heartbeat stops. It does not by itself mean that all other treatment, nutrition, medications, or symptom management must stop. Option C is correct. A and B overextend the order, while D fragments CPR into interventions the DNR is intended to withhold.
items.finding: Fresh audit made the distinction between DNR and global treatment limitation explicit without answer-length cueing.

items.source_name: HHS — HIPAA Privacy Rule: Personal Representatives
items.locator: 45 CFR 164.502(g), General Provisions/Who Must Be Recognized: a person authorized under applicable law to make health-care decisions is the individual's personal representative; a court-appointed legal guardian may have such authority, and the scope follows applicable law/order.
items.version: HHS guidance current in 2026; 45 CFR 164.502(g) authority and currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN 2026 Management of Care legal-rights check completed first.
items.stem: An incapacitated adult has a court-appointed guardian whose order specifically grants authority for the health care decision now required. A sibling demands to decide instead. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Recognize the guardian's authority within the court order and involve the client as much as the client's abilities allow.
options.B: Let the sibling make the decision because family preference overrides a court order granting health care authority.
options.C: Ignore the guardianship because court-appointed guardians are never permitted to make health care decisions.
options.D: Ask whichever relative is physically present to decide because presence determines temporary legal authority.

items.rationale: HHS explains that a person with legal authority to make health care decisions, including a court-appointed guardian when the order grants that authority, is the personal representative within the scope of that authority. Option A is correct. Family presence alone does not override legal authority, and guardianship authority must be respected rather than ignored.
items.finding: Round-2 review retained the primary HHS/45 CFR source and made all four legal-authority actions comparable in scope, removing the prior short-distractor cue.

items.source_name: American Association of Critical-Care Nurses — Critical Care Nurse Staffing Standards
items.locator: Critical-care staffing standards: critically ill/injured patients generally require about one nurse for every two patients; assignments must reflect patient needs/acuity, workload, and nurse competency, with additional support for nurses new to a unit.
items.version: AACN staffing standards published 2024-04-23 and current; live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN 2026 Management of Care assignment/competency check completed first.
items.stem: Which staffing principle is most appropriate for critically ill clients?

options.A: Match assignments to acuity, workload, and nurse competency; many critically ill clients require about one nurse for two patients.
options.B: Use the same routine patient load as a general medical-surgical unit because ICU acuity does not change staffing needs.
options.C: Assign every critically ill client permanently one-to-one regardless of condition, therapy, workload, or available support.
options.D: Use a fixed ratio alone without considering patient acuity, workload, nurse competency, or changes in clinical condition.

items.rationale: AACN staffing standards emphasize matching nursing assignments to current patient needs, workload, and nurse competency; critically ill patients generally require approximately one nurse for every two patients, with some requiring more intensive staffing. Option A is correct. B underestimates acuity, while C and D incorrectly make staffing an inflexible rule.
items.finding: Round-2 review made all four staffing approaches comparable in semantic detail without presenting the 1:2 concept as an absolute universal ratio.

items.locator: Treatment/Management: acute compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency; remove restrictive dressings/casts and obtain immediate surgical consultation; definitive treatment is urgent fasciotomy when indicated to prevent irreversible nerve and muscle ischemic injury.
items.version: Current StatPearls/NCBI Bookshelf Acute Compartment Syndrome entry live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A client is diagnosed with acute compartment syndrome of the lower leg. Which treatment should the nurse anticipate?

options.A: Observation with oral analgesics until swelling resolves.
options.C: Application of a tighter circumferential cast.
options.D: Vigorous massage of the affected extremity.

items.rationale: Acute compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency because rising compartment pressure can cause irreversible nerve and muscle ischemia. Urgent fasciotomy is the definitive decompressive treatment when indicated, making Option B correct. Observation, tighter compression, or massage can delay or worsen care.
items.finding: Fresh audit removed padded alternatives while preserving clinically plausible emergency-management distractors.

items.source_name: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS — Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report
items.locator: Potassium management in DKA: if potassium is below 3.5 mmol/L, begin potassium replacement and delay insulin until potassium rises above 3.5 mmol/L because insulin can worsen hypokalemia and precipitate arrhythmia/respiratory muscle weakness.
items.version: 2024 international consensus report, Diabetes Care 47(8):1257-1275; remains current and live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A client with diabetic ketoacidosis has a serum potassium level of 3.0 mmol/L before insulin is started. Which sequence is expected?

options.A: Start insulin immediately without potassium replacement because potassium will rise once hyperglycemia improves.
options.B: Give a potassium-wasting diuretic before insulin because reducing total body potassium improves DKA treatment.
options.C: Withhold fluids, potassium, and insulin until glucose falls below 250 mg/dL without treatment.
options.D: Begin potassium replacement and delay insulin until the potassium level rises above 3.5 mmol/L.

items.rationale: Current consensus guidance recommends potassium replacement when admission potassium is below 3.5 mmol/L and delaying insulin until potassium rises above 3.5 mmol/L. Option D is correct because insulin would shift potassium intracellularly and can worsen severe hypokalemia. A, B, and C increase risk or delay needed therapy.
items.finding: Round-2 review retained the current 2024 potassium threshold and rebuilt all four treatment sequences as comparable clinical actions, eliminating the keyed-option length cue.

items.locator: Differential diagnosis/clinical features: serotonin syndrome develops rapidly after serotonergic exposure/change and is characterized by neuromuscular hyperreactivity, especially hyperreflexia and clonus; NMS more often has marked rigidity and a slower onset.
items.version: StatPearls Serotonin Syndrome updated 2024-03-02 and current in StatPearls [Internet] 2026; live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: Which finding most strongly favors serotonin syndrome over neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

options.A: Lead-pipe rigidity and reduced reflexes developing gradually after exposure to a dopamine-blocking drug.
options.B: Hyperreflexia and clonus developing rapidly after a serotonergic medication is started or increased.
options.C: Flaccid weakness with absent clonus and no increase in reflexes after a medication change.
options.D: Fever without clonus, hyperreflexia, rigidity, or another characteristic neuromuscular finding.

items.rationale: Serotonin syndrome is distinguished by neuromuscular hyperreactivity, especially clonus and hyperreflexia, and often develops quickly after serotonergic exposure or a medication change. Option B is correct. Lead-pipe rigidity and slower evolution are more typical of NMS, while C and D lack the characteristic serotonin-syndrome neuromuscular findings.
items.finding: Round-2 review made all four diagnostic patterns comparable in detail while preserving the most discriminating neuromuscular features.
